titleEn: You are my shelter in the land of the living
progression: | Dm Dm | Gm Dm | A A | Dm Dm |
intro: Eight verses of one man talking, with the heading placing him in a cave. It is the smallest complete lament in the book: two verses of crying out, two of describing the situation, one of turning, one of asking, one of what happens afterwards. For a learner it is dense with the first person singular, the possessive suffix -i on nouns and the prefix a- on verbs, so almost every line says my something or I do something. Watch how the pronouns behave: the psalm speaks about God until verse 4, then says You and never goes back.

stichs.en: A maskil of David,
when he was in the cave. A prayer.

verses.summary: The heading gives a genre, an author, a circumstance and then a second genre label, which is unusual. Which cave is meant is not said.

stichs.en: With my voice I cry out to the LORD,
with my voice I plead with the LORD.

verses.summary: The same four slots twice with only the verb changed, which is the tightest parallelism in the psalm. Both verbs are unfinished action, so this is happening now, not being reported.

stichs.en: I pour out my complaint before Him,
I tell my trouble before Him.

verses.summary: The word order flips between the two lines, verb first then verb last, which frames the pair. Nothing is asked for yet: the speaker is still only describing what he is doing.

stichs.en: When my spirit grows faint within me,
You know my path.
On the road that I walk they have hidden a trap for me.

verses.summary: The turn to direct address happens inside the verse, and it happens at the lowest point rather than after it. The trappers are never named, only given a plural verb.

stichs.en: Look to the right and see:
there is no one who knows me.
Escape has vanished from me,
no one cares about my life.

verses.summary: The right hand is where a defender or a witness would stand, so the command is to check the empty seat. Three separate negations in one verse, which is the densest stretch of loneliness in the psalm.

stichs.en: I have cried out to You, LORD.
I have said: You are my shelter,
my portion in the land of the living.

verses.summary: The hinge. The verbs switch to completed action, so the speaker stops narrating the crisis and states what he has already decided. Portion is a land word, used of the share a family receives, which is pointed from a man with no ground of his own.

stichs.en: Listen closely to my cry,
for I am brought very low.
Rescue me from my pursuers,
for they are stronger than I am.

verses.summary: The first actual request arrives in verse 7 of 8, and it comes with two reasons attached, both of them admissions of weakness. The argument is not that he deserves rescue but that he cannot manage without it.

stichs.en: Bring my soul out of confinement
to give thanks to Your name.
Because of me the righteous will gather round,
for You will deal generously with me.

glosses: they will gather in a crown
verses.summary: The psalm ends with a room full of people, which is the exact opposite of verse 5. Nothing has changed in the situation; only the expected outcome has been stated.

pardes.body: A lament with all the standard parts and nothing extra. Verses 2 and 3 are the cry, described rather than quoted. Verses 4 and 5 are the situation: a spirit failing, a hidden trap, and the discovery that the place where a defender should stand is empty. Verse 6 is the turn, and it is marked grammatically as well as emotionally, the verbs switching to completed action for the first time. Verse 7 is the request, held back until almost the end, with two reasons given, both of them concessions of weakness. Verse 8 is the outcome, and it is the only verse with other people in it. Note what does not happen: the enemies are never named, no wrong is alleged against them, and the speaker never claims to be innocent.

Three places where the Hebrew is harder than any translation admits. The image in {{4.0}} is a verb of wrapping, so the spirit is muffled rather than merely weak, and the same idiom for a spirit wrapping itself over its owner recurs in Psalm 143:4. The imperative of {{5.0}} does not say who is being addressed: read as speech to God it is a challenge, read as speech to a bystander it is a man pointing at the space beside him, and translations split on it. The verb of {{8.7}} is the difficulty everyone agrees on: it is built on the root for crown, and it is variously rendered as the righteous will crown themselves, will crown me, will surround me, or will gather about me. The choice changes who is honoured in the last line of the psalm, and the text does not decide it.

The heading at {{1.3}} invites the psalm to be read against the narratives in 1 Samuel where David hides in a cave, the escape to Adullam in chapter 22 and the encounter with Saul at En Gedi in chapter 24. The text does not say which, and both have been proposed. Reading it against chapter 24 is the sharper option: there David is the one holding a hiding place while his pursuer walks in unaware, so the man praying that there is no escape for him is, at that moment, the one with the advantage. That gap between the felt situation and the actual one is what the tradition takes from the psalm, along with the fact that {{6.5}} is spoken from inside a cave, where shelter is exactly what a man already has and still does not trust.

The mystical reading takes {{8.1}}, the confinement, as the body and the exile rather than a prison of stone, and the soul brought out of it as the soul returning to a range of movement it lost rather than escaping a place. On that reading the portion in the land of the living in verse 6 is not survival but an allotment in a world that does not end, claimed by a man who at that moment owns nothing at all. The cave then does double duty: the narrow place a person is pressed into, and the enclosure inside which a prayer becomes audible because there is nowhere else for the voice to go.
